metas.name: Albania - Cylinder Water Tanks
metas.note:
• You will see a lot of cylinder-shaped water tanks on the roofs of buildings.

--- NOTE:

  • This is less common in Montenegro.
  • Some parts of Turkey also have a lot of similar-looking water tanks.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - Italian Style Buildings
metas.note:
Albania has a lot of Italian-style buildings:

  • Pastel colours, orange tiled roofs, and blocky shapes with lots of balconies.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Andorra - Stone Buildings
metas.note:
• Andorra has a lot of these stone buildings.
  • They can be seen almost everywhere in the country.

--- NOTE:

  • These buildings can also be found close to Andorra, in the French and Spanish Pyrenees.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/andorra.

metas.name: Argentina - Jujuy - Red Bricks
metas.note: • Red bricks, similar to what is common in Bolivia, can be found in the northwest of the country, especially in western Jujuy.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/argentina.

metas.name: Austria - Alpine Architecture
metas.note:
• Alpine architecture is common in Austria and other countries in the Alps.
  • Houses commonly have distinct light coloured walls, with wooden elements such as balconies or panelling around the top floor, with dark-coloured wooden roofs that extend outward.

--- NOTE:

  • Germany uses similar architecture in its southern states.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/austria.

metas.name: Azores - White & Pastel Colors
metas.note:
• Houses in the Azores are typically one or two stories, with an orange tiled roof.
  • They are painted white or in pastel colours, and dark green shutters on windows are common.

--- NOTE:

  • While you can also find yellow or blue highlights like in mainland Portugal, grey highlights are almost exclusive to the Azores.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Belgium - Red Bricks
metas.note:
• A lot of houses in Belgium are made of distinctive red bricks.

--- NOTE:

  • This is more common in the North and West of the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Belgium - South - Gray Tone Stones
metas.note: • Houses in the South of the country use a lot of stone, have gray tones and generally look more French.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Bermuda - Hamilton
metas.note: • Hamilton is by far the largest town on Bermuda, and as such, the downtown area is distinct due to its many large, densely built multi-floor buildings.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Bermuda - White Roofs
metas.note:
• Most buildings on Bermuda are single family stone houses painted in pastel colours.
  • They will almost always have completely white roofs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Bhutan - Unique Architecture
metas.note:
• The traditional Bhutanese architecture is very distinct.
  • Most of the houses have tin roofs and wooden painted frames, which give them a unique look.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bhutan.

metas.name: Bolivia - Unfinished Look
metas.note:
• Many buildings in Bolivia consist of large red bricks.
  • Buildings often have an ‘unfinished' look.

--- NOTE:

  • This style of architecture is also common in parts of Peru.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bolivia.

metas.name: Botswana - Shacks & Bungalows
metas.note:
• Typical Botswana houses range from small impoverished shacks to comfortable middle-class bungalows.
  • Some buildings have exposed grey bricks.
  • On occasion, you might find traditional round huts.

--- NOTE:

  • All of these house styles are also found in the other southern African countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/botswana.

metas.name: Brazil - Acre - Houses On Stilts
metas.note:
• Wooden houses on stilts are very common in the state of Acre.

--- NOTE:

  • They are also seen more rarely in low-lying Amazonas and Pará, as well as various other countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Orange Tiled Roofs
metas.note: • Many houses throughout Brazil have orange tiled roofs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Santa Catarina - European Influence
metas.note: • Buildings in the southern states, mainly Santa Catarina, can be of European influence (typically vaguely German) in design and style.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Bulgaria - Ghetto-Like Look
metas.note: • Suburbs in Bulgaria are generally among the poorest areas in Europe, with small, densely built houses and generally an almost ghetto-like look.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Bulgaria - Patches Of Mortar
metas.note:
• Most houses in Bulgaria have orange tiled roofs, with distinct patches of mortar along the corner tiles.

Famously, Bulgarian roofs often seem poorly constructed:

  • The roof tiles and mortar tend to be uneven, especially when compared to other European countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Bulgaria - South - Alpine Architecture
metas.note: • Buildings with features similar to Alpine architecture, such as white walls with brown wooden details are commonly found in and around the Smoljan region in the south.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Cambodia - Blue Windows
metas.note:
Traditional Cambodian wooden stilt houses tend to have very recognizable colour schemes:

  • Walls are commonly painted dark red-brown, light blue or an ochre orange.
  • Doors, windows and other architectural details are often painted bright blue.

--- NOTE:

  • More modern houses tend to have a wider variety of colour schemes.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/cambodia.

metas.name: Cambodia - Stilts & Double Roofs
metas.note:
• Wooden houses on stilts are common.
  • Walls are often made of vertical planks.
  • Many homes have double or triple roofs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/cambodia.

metas.name: Cambodia - Temples
metas.note:
• The majority of Cambodians are Buddhist.
  • Temples are common throughout the country.
  • Temple architecture is highly decorative, with ornamented roofs.

--- NOTE:

  • Thailand and Laos are also majority Buddhist.
  • Temples in these countries can look similar.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/cambodia.

metas.name: Cambodia - Tiled & Red Roofs
metas.note:
• Many traditional homes have tiled orange or red roofs, sometimes with ornaments on the ridges and corners.
  • Corrugated and plain metal roofs are also common.
  • On other, more modern buildings, you can see a wider variety of roof colours and materials.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/cambodia.

metas.name: Croatia - Adriatic Coast - Beige Bricks
metas.note:
• Houses and walls made of beige brick are common on the Adriatic coast.
  • They often feature green shutters.

--- NOTE:

  • Similar architecture can also be found in some regions in Italy.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/croatia.

metas.name: Croatia - Red Brick Walls
metas.note:
• Buildings in Croatia sometimes feature exposed red brick walls.
  • This architecture is more common in inland areas.

--- NOTE:

  • This type of architecture can also be found in Slovenia and Serbia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/croatia.

metas.name: Curaçao - One Storey Bungalows
metas.note:
• Much of the architecture on Curaçao consists of simple, one storey bungalows that are pastel coloured.
  • Metal roofs are common on smaller shacks, while tiled roofs can be seen on more expensive houses.
  • Additionally, multi storey villas can sometimes be seen.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Czechia - České Budějovice - Baroque Architecture
metas.note:
• A variant of baroque architecture called Selské Baroko (folk baroque) can be found in the region surrounding České Budějovice.
  • The style is characterised by highly decorated walls, with the setting being small villages rather than towns and cities.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Diamond Shaped Tiles
metas.note:
• Roofs with diamond shaped tiles are common in both Czechia and Slovakia.

--- NOTE:

  • This is also somewhat common in Hungary.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Moravia - Architecture
metas.note:
Town houses in Moravia typically have two distinctive features:

  • Houses have the long side parallel to the road and are often connected in large groups.
  • Front doors are abnormally large, similar in size and shape to barn doors.

--- NOTE:

  • This is also common in northeastern Austria.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - North - Dark Wooden Supports
metas.note: • Houses with thick, dark wooden poles supporting the upper floors are common in the northernmost parts of the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - North - Timber Framed Houses
metas.note: • Timber framed houses in Czechia are mostly found along the northern parts of the German border.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - North - White Stripes
metas.note: • Dark wooden houses, with white stripes shining through the wood, are common in most of northern Czechia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Northwest - Single Pane Windows
metas.note: • It is more common to see houses with single pane windows in the northwestern parts of the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Pair Houses
metas.note:
• Suburban houses in Czechia are commonly connected in pairs.

--- NOTE:

  • This is less common in most neighbouring countries, including Slovakia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Czechia - Prefabricated Panel Apartments
metas.note:
• Like all of the former Eastern bloc, prefabricated panel apartment buildings are a common sight in urban areas.
  • What distinguishes Czechia and Slovakia is the relatively good maintenance often combined with vibrant colours and patterns.

--- NOTE:

  • To a lesser extent, you can find this kind of architecture in neighbouring countries, like Poland and Hungary.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/czechia.

metas.name: Denmark - Red Bricks
metas.note:
• Much of the architecture in Denmark consists of red brick.
  • Roofs often have orange, dark brown or black tiles.

--- NOTE:

  • Similar brick architecture is also common in the Netherlands and Belgium.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Denmark - Thatched & Corrugated Roofs
metas.note:
• Some houses in Denmark have thatched roofs, especially in rural areas.
  • You can also sometimes find grey corrugated roofs.
  • These look somewhat similar to roofs commonly found in Baltic countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Denmark - Timer Frame Walls
metas.note:
• Some older or rural buildings have timber frame walls.

--- NOTE:

  • Timber framing can be found in other Western and Central European countries as well, but are an especially common wall type for historical buildings in Denmark.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/denmark.

metas.name: Ecuador - Grey Bricks
metas.note:
• Most houses are made of grey bricks and have metal roofs.

--- NOTE:

  • This is not unique to Ecuador, but is very common.
  • Countries such as Peru, and especially Bolivia, commonly use red bricks.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ecuador.

metas.name: Estonia - Wood & White Brick
metas.note:
• Estonian architecture generally consists of a combination of wood and white brick, typically with somewhat steep corrugated metal roofs.
  • Painted stone walls are also somewhat common.
  • While wooden buildings can be found in all three Baltic countries, they are more common in Estonia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Faroe Islands - Above Ground Basements
metas.note:
• Faroese houses are typically made of wood, often with an above ground basement made of stone which is painted in a different colour than the wooden part.
  • Roofs will usually be either metal or have grass on top (turf).
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Finland - Modern & Utilitarian Architecture
metas.note:
• Finnish architecture is mostly modern and utilitarian.
  • Downtown areas tend to be very modern, with lots of apartment buildings and use of concrete.
  • Suburbs mostly consist of freestanding single family homes.
  • Like Sweden and Norway, some wooden buildings, especially in the countryside, are painted in a distinctive dark red colour.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/finland.

metas.name: France - Alps - Alpine Architecture
metas.note:
• Alpine architecture, unmistakable for its light coloured base and extensive wooden elements, is unsurprisingly found in the Alps.

--- NOTE:

  • Similar houses can be found in the touristic parts of Pyrenees.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Alsace - Germanic Architecture
metas.note:
• Many elements of Germanic architecture are concentrated in Alsace, such as timber framing and half-hip roof.
  • Furthermore, roofs with fish scale tiles are more common in this region.
  • Beware that these elements are sometimes incorporated into architecture in other parts of France, and are most reliable in conjunction with one another.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Basque - Colorful Timber Framing
metas.note:
• White houses with, often colourful, timber framing are a staple of Basque architecture that extends beyond the Basque speaking area.
  • The timber frame colour (in this case red) will be consistent with other wooden elements, like window shutters and gates.

--- NOTE:

  • They’re also common in parts of Northern Spain, where the timber frames are usually unpainted.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Belgian Border - Dark Red Bricks
metas.note:
• Rows of dark red brick houses, most similar to Flemish architecture in Belgium, are unsurprisingly found near the Belgian border.
  • The individual bricks may be outlined by white mortar.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Brittany - Architecture
metas.note:
• Brittany has one of the most recognizable and consistent architectures in the country.
  • Common elements include, in addition to black roofs, edge chimneys, black slate walls and stones surrounding doors and windows.
  • The walls will be either very light coloured or made of stone.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - French Riviera - Architecture
metas.note:
• The French Riviera will mirror many characteristics of Monaco.
  • Rich areas with planted palms and light coloured multi story buildings with wide balconies are good indications you’re in this area, with the rest of the southern coast and Corsican Bastia sharing similar vibes.

--- NOTE:

  • Just like Monaco, several cities host boat trekkers in their harbour.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - General Architecture
metas.note:
• French architecture largely consists of stone houses, which will normally be either unpainted or painted in greyish or yellow pastel colours.
  • The roofs will typically have a simple gable design, with orange tiles or less commonly black slates.

--- NOTE:

  • Do note that France has some of the most diverse regional architecture of any European country, so don’t be surprised to see towns that look significantly different from the previously described architecture.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Northwest - Black Shingle Roofs
metas.note:
• Black shingle roofs are primarily found in the northwest, the rough cutoff being the Loire river.
  • Other areas include near the Belgian border, the south-centre, and the Pyrenees, making black roofs a good clue for Alps-Pyrenees toss-ups.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Paris - Uneven & Cream Colored Stones
metas.note:
• Walls made of uneven cream coloured to orange stones, glued with mortar and often incorporating red brick details can be found in the towns surrounding Paris.
  • Note that the city of Paris itself generally does not have this architecture.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - South - Rounded Tiles
metas.note: • Roofs in the south of the country will often be made up of rounded tiles overlapping one another, often varying in colour.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Toulouse - Architecture
metas.note:
• In and around Toulouse, mainly in old towns, you will commonly find bright orange brick buildings.
  • They differ from brick houses near Belgium by the bricks being brighter, as well as somewhat Mediterranean looking architectural features, such as wooden shutters, being common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Germany - Central - Black Fish Scale Roofs & Walls
metas.note: • Houses with black slate walls, resembling fish scales, are commonly found in a large area of central Germany.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - East - Large Apartment Buildings
metas.note: • These large, utilitarian apartment buildings constructed during the socialist era, that are also known as “Commie blocks” are common in all of former East Germany.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - Northwest - Brick Houses
metas.note:
• These brick houses are generally concentrated in northwestern Germany.

--- NOTE:

  • This map is very approximate.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - Schleswig-Holstein - Thatched Roofs
metas.note:
• Thatched roofs and rock walls are most common on the North Frisian Islands, as well as mainland Schleswig-Holstein.
  • You can also commonly find them in coastal resort towns in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Greece - Cyclade Islands - White Walls & Blue Doors
metas.note:
One of the most well-known types of Greek architecture:

  • Houses with completely white walls, blue doors and shutters, is mainly found on the small central Cyclade islands.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - Mediterranean Architecture
metas.note:
Greek architecture shares a lot of features with other Mediterranean countries:

  • A lot of white and pastel-coloured stone houses with orange tiled roofs.
  • White houses are very common when compared to most other Mediterranean countries.
  • Urban residential buildings will generally be multi-floored, light-coloured and typically have connected balconies along one or multiple walls.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - Thessaloniki - Tall Antennas
metas.note: • In Thessaloniki, you will often see a large amount of unusually tall antennas on top of buildings.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greenland - Colorful Wooden Houses
metas.note:
• Greenlandic architecture mainly consists of small, colourful, simple looking wooden houses, which even in cities are typically placed quite sparsely.
  • The major cities have some larger buildings, which normally look fairly minimalistic.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Guatemala - Pastel Stone Houses
metas.note:
• Guatemalan architecture mainly consists of pastel painted stone houses, commonly with rusted sheet metal roofs.
  • It is also somewhat common for buildings to be made out of exposed white brick.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/guatemala.

metas.name: Hongkong - Tall Apartment Buildings
metas.note:
• One very striking aspect of Hong Kong architecture are the many extremely tall apartment buildings found throughout the city.

--- NOTE:

  • Apartment buildings in Singapore and Taiwan tend to be not nearly as tall as those in Hong Kong.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Hungary - Red Tiles Roofs & Light Colors
metas.note:
• Hungarian houses are typically made of stone, painted in a light colour and almost always with red tiled roofs.
  • Suburban houses are typically only one storeyed, while more central houses may be taller.
  • Houses in town and city centres are often fairly old but well-kept.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/hungary.

metas.name: India - Central - Rounded Roof Tiles
metas.note:
• Rounded roof tiles are common in central India.
  • They often appear disorganised and are kept in rows/columns that are not completely straight.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - East Coast - Thatched Roofs
metas.note:
• Houses or huts with thatched roofs are mainly found along the east coast and northern plains.
  • Large hay mounds are also generally more common in this region.

--- NOTE:

  • Thatched roofs from Uttar Pradesh to Odisha tend to be made of fine pieces of hay whereas thatched roofs from Odisha to Tamil Nadu tend to be made of dried palm fans.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - Goa & Kerala - Modern Homes
metas.note: • Goa and Kerala are two of the most developed states in India and often have very wealthy and modern homes.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - Northeast - Square Panels
metas.note: • Houses made of square panels separated by thin beams are found in Northeast India.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - Northeast - Triangle Metal Roofs
metas.note: • Metal roofs, with a small triangle near the top, are common in Northeast India.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - Punjab - White Domes
metas.note:
• Gurdwaras, which can typically be recognised by their white domes and ornate walls, are most common in Punjab.
  • You can also sometimes recognise them by the Sikh Khanda symbol, which represents the religion.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - South - Organized Tiles
metas.note:
• Roofs in southern India are characterised by more organised tiles that are bright orange and flat with a ridge in the middle.
  • It is particularly common in Tamil Nadu.

--- NOTE:

  • Similarly shaped tiles with a darker brown colour are common further north.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - West Bengal - Diamond Protrusion
metas.note: • Flat roof tiles, similar to the ones found in the south, with a small diamond shaped protrusion in the middle, are commonly found in and around West Bengal.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - West Bengal - Metal Hip Roofs
metas.note: • Large hip roofs made of corrugated sheet metal are found in West Bengal and adjacent areas in Bihar and Odisha.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: Indonesia - Bali - Architecture
metas.note:
• Architecture in Bali is unique because it was influenced by old Balinese culture and Hinduism.
  • The most important thing to look for are these crown-like roof pinnacles, found everywhere in Bali.
  • Guardian statues and slit-drum towers are common too.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - Churches
metas.note: • Indonesia is religiously a Muslim majority country, so seeing churches, and other Christian signs, is a good clue for these regions.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - Gable Horns
metas.note:
• Roofs with gable horns can be found most commonly in South Sulawesi, Riau and Central and South Kalimantan.

--- NOTE:

  • Horned roofs are often found with Bugis roofs in South Sulawesi.
  • Use this tip along with other clues to determine which region you are in.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - Java - Tiled Roofs
metas.note:
• Tiled roofs are most commonly found on the island of Java, and sometimes nearby regions such as southern Sumatra, the Lesser Sunda Islands, and South Kalimantan.

--- NOTE:

  • The tiles on roofs in South Kalimantan and Jambi look slightly different.
  • The tiles are usually less rounded but flatter.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - Kalimantan - Wooden Chips
metas.note: • On Kalimantan, you can find these unique roofs made out of wooden chips.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - North - Plain Sheet Metal Roofs
metas.note:
• Plain sheet metal roofs are more commonly found toward the north, where tiled roofs are not found.
  • They are most commonly found on Kalimantan, Sulawesi and Sumatra.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - North Sumatra - Boat Roofs
metas.note:
• North Sumatra features similarly distinct boat-shaped roofs, however the roofs are less angled upward and they do not feature spires.

--- NOTE:

  • These roofs are most commonly found near Lake Toba, due to its sacred history.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - Rante Pao - Tongkonan
metas.note:
• A small region of South Sulawesi, around the city of Rante Pao, features these very unique houses, called Tongkonan, that have saddle-shaped roofs.
  • The houses themselves are also elevated from the ground.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - South Sulawesi - Slots Inside Triangles
metas.note:
• These horizontal slots inside the triangles of the roofs are almost unique to Southern Sulawesi.

--- NOTE:

  • They can rarely be found in East Kalimantan and West Nusa.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - Sumba - High-Pitched Peaks
metas.note: • You can find these distinct roofs with uniquely high-pitched peaks on Sumba.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - West Sumatra - Boat Roofs
metas.note: • West Sumatra features these distinct boat-shaped roofs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Ireland - Cream Colors & Black Roofs
metas.note:
• You will usually find cream white buildings with black roofs in Ireland.
  • Sometimes, the buildings feature grey corner stones.
  • In cities, you will typically find row buildings.

--- NOTE:

  • British style brick buildings can still be found in Ireland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Isle Of Man - Whitewashed Walls
metas.note: • Houses with whitewashed walls and entrance walls are a common sight, similar to Ireland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Israel - Blocky Buildings
metas.note:
• Architecture tends to consist of bright and warm-coloured stone buildings, often with a blocky appearance.
  • While Mediterranean-style houses with orange tiled roofs are more common than in other Middle Eastern countries, flat roofs are still just as common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/israel-west-bank.

metas.name: Italy - Alps - Alpine Architecture
metas.note: • Alpine architecture, which typically features large buildings with white stone walls and wooden details, are found in the Alpine region.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Aosta Valley - Grey Uneven Bricks
metas.note:
• Buildings in Aosta Valley are often built with grey uneven bricks, with an Alpine look.

--- NOTE:

  • This can look superficially similar to Andorran architecture.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Apulian - Flat Roofs
metas.note:
• Houses in the Apulian region are generally very light coloured, and have flat roofs, typically with two to three floors.
  • The architecture is sometimes reminiscent of the Middle East.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - General Architecture
metas.note:
• Italian architecture mainly consists of pastel coloured stone houses, generally with terracotta roofs.
  • Houses will very commonly have wooden shutters, which will typically be divided in two and open sideways.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Northeast - Solid Wooden Shutters
metas.note: • Solid wooden shutters with black metal hinges is a common feature in the northeast of Italy, particularly in Veneto.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Southeast - Trullo Roofs
metas.note:
• This particular style of roof, called a trullo, is unique to the Itria valley in southeastern Italy.
  • It is particularly common in and around the town of Alberobello.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Tuscany - Unpainted Bricks
metas.note:
• A lot of buildings in and around Tuscany are made of irregular unpainted brown-grey bricks.

--- NOTE:

  • A similar style of architecture can be found in northeastern Spain.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Japan - Chugoku - Red Tiled Roofs
metas.note: • These unique red-tiled roofs are most commonly found in Chugoku, especially in the prefectures of Hiroshima and Shimane.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/japan.

metas.name: Japan - General Architecture
metas.note:
• Japanese architecture has many distinct and expressive styles, with many unique buildings.
  • These can range from traditional country houses, regional designs, modern large cities, coastal reinforced buildings, and anything in between.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/japan.

metas.name: Japan - North & South - Roof Transition
metas.note:
• The further you are north, roofs generally transition from tiled to level or flat sloped in order to compensate for heavy snowfall.
  • Northern houses often have ladders attached to the side, giving roof access to clear snow.

--- NOTE:

  • In addition to north to south, high-elevation mountainous regions or high snowfall areas often use such roofs, even in more central or southern prefectures.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/japan.

metas.name: Japan - Okinawa - White Buildings & Flat Roofs
metas.note: • Okinawa can often be recognised by the white concrete buildings with flat roofs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/japan.

metas.name: Jersey - Northern France Architecture
metas.note:
• Similarly, the local architecture shares many characteristics with that of northern France.
  • This includes pastel-coloured walls and dark slate roofs.
  • However, British-style terraced houses are also common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Jersey - Red Granite
metas.note:
• Jersey is home to large reserves of red granite.
  • As a result, it is a popular building material used for the construction of many walls and houses throughout the island.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Jordan - Sandstone Bricks
metas.note:
• Most buildings in Jordan are made of bright sandstone bricks and have flat roofs.

--- NOTE:

  • Similar sandstone bricks are also common in Jerusalem and in the West Bank.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/jordan.

metas.name: Laos - Historical Architecture
metas.note:
• Luang Prabang is the former royal capital of Laos and a UNESCO heritage site.
  • The city has a lot of historical architecture, including several temples.
  • Many buildings make use of traditional dark wooden architectural elements.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/laos.

metas.name: Latvia - White Bricks & Corrugated Roofs
metas.note:
• Latvian architecture generally consists of a combination of wood and white brick, typically with somewhat steep corrugated metal roofs.
  • Slightly modern houses with pastel coloured stone walls and houses with a combination of wood with another material, particularly white brick, are also common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/latvia.

metas.name: Lesotho - Round Huts
metas.note:
• In rural areas, you will often see traditional round huts with thatched roofs.

--- NOTE:

  • These are less common in the other three southern African countries, but can still be seen.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lesotho.

metas.name: Lithuania - Light Colored Bricks
metas.note:
• Lithuanian architecture primarily consists of light coloured brick buildings, usually with somewhat steep corrugated metal roofs.
  • Wooden buildings are also fairly common, however less so than in Estonia.
  • Pastel painted stone buildings are somewhat common, especially in newer suburbs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Luxembourg - Dark Slate Roofs
metas.note:
• Houses tend to have dark slate roofs.
  • Walls and windows tend to be plain and undecorated.
  • Walls are usually painted white, grey, or pastel colours.

--- NOTE:

  • Such architecture can also be found in the surrounding regions in Belgium and France, but is especially prominent in Luxembourg.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/luxembourg.

metas.name: Macao - Dense Buildings
metas.note: • Dense apartment buildings with gridded, narrow streets and cars parked on both sides can be found in this region in the northern half of Macau.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Madeira - White, Yellow & Pink Painting
metas.note:
• Houses are mainly painted white, grey, or pastel colours such as yellow and pink.
  • In addition, the red tile roofs will often be in a good condition.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Malta - Covered Balconies
metas.note:
• This style of traditional covered balconies is very common on Maltese buildings.
  • They are often painted in bright colours.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malta.

metas.name: Malta - Low Storey Buildings
metas.note:
• The vast majority of buildings in Malta consist of low storey buildings, with white to beige coloured walls.
  • Buildings made of limestone are also fairly common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malta.

metas.name: Mexico - Durango - Mud Bricks
metas.note:
• Mud brick buildings are most abundant in Durango, especially full houses constructed with mud brick.
  • However, they can essentially be found in almost all of the dry desert states.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - East - White Concrete Blocks
metas.note:
• White concrete block buildings are highly concentrated in the states surrounding Mexico city, and are generally more common to the east.
  • They can however still be found all over the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - North - American Style Bungalows
metas.note:
• Architecture in northern Mexico often features design elements from American style bungalows.
  • Many houses are coloured with light or pastel colours, gated and commonly have front yards.
  • Orange tiles inspired by Spanish colonial architecture are also typical.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - West - Red Bricks
metas.note: • Red brick buildings are mostly concentrated in the states west of Mexico City, specifically Jalisco, Michoacan, Guanajuato, and Aguascalientes.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - Yucatan - Light Colored Rocks
metas.note: • These walls made of light coloured rock are found in the Yucatan peninsula, but most common in Yucatan state.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - Yucatan - Thatched Roofs
metas.note:
• Thatched roofs are most common in the Yucatan peninsula and eastern San Luis Potosi.
  • They can also be found elsewhere, mainly in the southeast.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Monaco - Luxurious Architecture
metas.note:
• Monaco is a rich and densely populated city state, with a Mediterranean feel to it.
  • The architecture is similar to cities in southern France and northern Italy, but more luxurious.
  • You will see a lot of apartment buildings, neoclassical details, and pastel colours.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/monaco.

metas.name: Netherlands - North - Very Large Roofs
metas.note: • Farms in the north of the Netherlands often have very large roofs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - Red-Brownish Bricks
metas.note:
• Brick architecture is very common in the Netherlands.
  • Many buildings feature red-brownish-coloured bricks.
  • Roofs often have orange or dark grey tiles.

--- NOTE:

  • Similar brick architecture is also common in Denmark and Belgium.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - Row Houses
metas.note:
• As mentioned before, row houses are very common in the Netherlands.
  • Almost half of the Dutch housing stock are row houses, significantly more than almost all other European countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - South - Rolling Shutters
metas.note:
• Rolling shutters on house windows are more common in the southern half of the Netherlands.

--- NOTE:

  • While more prevalent in the south, rolling shutters on homes in more northern regions are not unheard of.
  • Use this meta with some caution.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Nigeria - Steeply Pitched Roofs
metas.note:
• Most Nigerian houses are single-storey, with steeply pitched roofs commonly made of metal sheets.
  • Cinder block walls surrounding the houses are also common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/nigeria.

metas.name: Norway - Black & White Houses
metas.note:
• The vast majority of Norwegian houses are made of wood.
  • Many houses are painted red, which is also typical for Sweden and Finland.
  • Black painted houses are also quite common, more so than in Sweden or Finland.

--- NOTE:

  • Sweden and Finland generally have more red and yellow houses, while Norway generally has more white houses.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - Grass Roofs
metas.note:
• Traditional houses in Norway commonly have grass covered roofs.

--- NOTE:

  • This is far less common in Sweden and Finland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Norway - South Coast - Full White Wooden Houses
metas.note: • While completely white wooden houses can be found in the entire country, they’re especially common on the southern coast, where you’ll commonly see entire villages made up of them.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/norway.

metas.name: Oman - Light-Colored Stone
metas.note:
• Buildings in Oman are typically made of light-coloured stone.
  • The houses are ‘blocky’ but still quite ornate, and they are usually surrounded by a matching fence, which often has an even more ornate gate.

--- NOTE:

  • Buildings in the UAE are often very similar.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/oman.

metas.name: Panama - Spanish Influence
metas.note:
• Panamanian architecture often reflects Spanish colonial influences, featuring vibrant colours, and some ornate detailing.
  • The most common type of building has painted concrete or sometimes brick walls with red metal sheets or tiles for a roof.
  • Many windows have bars on them for security.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/panama.

metas.name: Peru - Diverse Architecture
metas.note:
• Peru is home to diverse and somewhat unique architecture.

Here are a few examples of types of buildings commonly seen in Peru:

  • Ranging from Colonial-era buildings, contemporary “boxy” buildings, and traditional red brick buildings.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/peru.

metas.name: Peru - North - Overhanging Roofs
metas.note:
• Buildings with overhanging roofs with wooden supports are mostly found in northern regions of Peru.
  • These buildings are sometimes brightly coloured as well.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/peru.

metas.name: Peru - South - Red Brick Transition
metas.note:
• As a general rule, the closer you are to Lake Titicaca in Peru, houses and buildings made out of red brick become more common.
  • This type of architecture resembles the predominant type of building seen in parts of western Bolivia, which is helpful for remembering where it is seen most commonly.

--- NOTE:

  • Red brick buildings can be seen anywhere in the country, so use other clues before guessing.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/peru.

metas.name: Philippines - Marawi - Destroyed Houses
metas.note: • In and around the city of Marawi, Mindanao you can find many destroyed houses and ruins from the Marawi siege in 2017.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/philippines.

metas.name: Philippines - Palawan - Diagonal Woven Pattern
metas.note: • Houses built with amakan walls (referred to as Sawali in the north) with a diagonally woven pattern are mostly found on the island of Palawan, but can also be found throughout the northern half of the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/philippines.

metas.name: Philippines - South - Diamond Pattern
metas.note: • Houses built with amakan walls, a traditionally woven bamboo mat, with a diamond pattern are almost exclusively found in the southern half of the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/philippines.

metas.name: Poland - East - Traditional Wooden Houses
metas.note: • Traditional wooden houses are commonly found in the east, mainly in Podlaskie Voivodeship.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Poland - General Architecture
metas.note:
• Buildings usually have plain stone walls covered in light or pastel stucco.
  • Frequent roofing colours are orange or red, black, and brown.
  • Roof tiles and panes often have a tidy, almost plastic-like look.
  • Some rural houses have corrugated sheet roofs similar to those often found in the Baltics.
  • Detached single family homes are common throughout Poland.
  • They sometimes have a blocky look.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Poland - General Architecture #2
metas.note:
• In bigger towns, apartment buildings are common.
  • Many date from communist times, and some of them still have a somewhat austere look.
  • However, many have been renovated and look nice and well-kept.
  • Downtown areas are usually dense and often have historic buildings.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Portugal - Blue / Yellow Paints
metas.note: • You’ll commonly see blue or yellow lines painted around windows and doors, as well as around the edges of walls.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Mosaic Tiles
metas.note: • Houses made of decorative mosaic tiles are somewhat common in Portugal.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - North - Square Blocks & White Mortar
metas.note:
• Houses in northern Portugal are often made of square concrete blocks, which are commonly put together with white mortar.

--- NOTE:

  • Very similar architecture, but typically without the white mortar, is commonly found over the border in Galicia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - White Stone & Orange Roofs
metas.note: • White painted stone houses with orange tiled roofs are extremely common in Portugal.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Romania - East - Metal & Fake Tiled Roofs
metas.note: • If you see several houses and almost all of them have metal or plastic fake tiled roofs, you will probably be in the eastern half of the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - Hungarian Border - Hungarian Style
metas.note:
• Villages near the Hungarian border will often be built in the same style as villages in Hungary.
  • This style can be summarised as having long, straight streets with single-storey houses being evenly spaced along the road, typically having the short side of the house facing the road.
  • The vast majority of roofs will have orange tiles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - Maramureș - Decorated Wooden Gates
metas.note: • Elaborately decorated wooden gates are commonly found in the region of Maramureș.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - Single Family Houses
metas.note:
• Romanian architecture primarily consists of single-family houses made of stone, typically painted in different pastel colours and with roofs ranging from orange tiles to grey metal.
  • It is also somewhat common to see houses with walls made of painted square tiles in different patterns.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - West - Orange Tiled Roofs
metas.note: • If you see several houses and almost all of them have orange tiled roofs, you are likely to be in the western half of the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Russia - Dagestan - Limestone Bricks
metas.note: • Buildings made of white limestone brick are indicative of Dagestan, as well as adjacent regions.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - Decorated Window Frames
metas.note:
• This style of richly decorated window frames is commonly found on traditional Russian homes, especially on log cabins.
  • They are often painted blue.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - Rectangular Apartments
metas.note:
• The vast majority of urban housing in Russia are large rectangular apartment buildings made of simple concrete.
  • Newer buildings in wealthier areas appear more modern.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - Rural Housing
metas.note: • Rural housing in Russia consists mostly of a basic wooden structure with metal roofs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Russia - South - Red Bricks
metas.note: • Buildings built almost entirely of red brick are mostly found south, but other notable exceptions include Magnitogorsk, Orsk, and Omsk.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Rwanda - Ventilation Bricks
metas.note:
• Rwandan architecture features a lot of brick and concrete.
  • Most houses in Rwanda are single family houses, which can have rather steep roofs. Houses also often have fences for protection.
  • The most notable feature of Rwandan architecture are the ‘ventilation bricks,’ which are present in many houses.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/rwanda.

metas.name: Slovakia - Diamond Shaped Tiles
metas.note:
• Roofs with diamond shaped tiles are common in both Slovakia and Czechia.

--- NOTE:

  • This is also somewhat common in Hungary.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - East - Grey Metal Roofs
metas.note:
• Grey metal roofs are very common, particularly in the eastern parts of Slovakia.

--- NOTE:

  • Apart from the most mountainous areas, it is far less common in Czechia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Hip End
metas.note:
• Many Slovak houses have the short side facing the road with the roof ending in a hip end.

--- NOTE:

  • This is also very common in Hungary, but less common in Czechia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia - Prefabricated Panel Apartments
metas.note:
• Like all of the former Eastern bloc, prefabricated panel apartment buildings are a common sight in urban areas.
  • What distinguishes Slovakia and Czechia is the relatively good maintenance often combined with vibrant colours and patterns.
  • Some smaller buildings also adhere to this style.

--- NOTE:

  • To a lesser extent, you can find this kind of architecture in neighbouring countries, like Poland and Hungary.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovenia - Alpine Architecture
metas.note:
• Slovenian architecture takes much inspiration from alpine architecture, with light coloured walls, dark wooden details and semi-steep roofs.
  • The most common roof shape is half-hipped roofs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovenia.

metas.name: South Korea - Red Bricks
metas.note: • Red brick is a very common building material in South Korea.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/south-korea.

metas.name: South Korea - Traditional Tiled Roofs
metas.note:
• Many buildings have traditional tiled roofs like these.
  • These often have decorative elements on the corners, and tend to have sides that curve slightly upwards.
  • Blue roofs are quite common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/south-korea.

metas.name: Spain - Asturias - Square Hórreos
metas.note:
• In Asturias, “hórreos” are bigger, generally with a square design, and are built above four pillars, with or without walls.
  • You will sometimes find a rectangular variation, usually built on top of six or eight pillars called “panera”.
  • If you find an “horreo” with a slate roof, you will be in western Asturias.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Balearic - Full White Houses
metas.note:
• The stereotypical Balearic house is painted completely white.
  • You can find flat roofs, but tiled roofs with a small incline are the most common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Basque - White Houses
metas.note: • Large white houses with wooden frames are common in the Basque Country, the Basque part of Navarra, and Cantabria.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Catalonia & Aragón - Masias
metas.note:
• Traditional farm houses called “masías” are common in Catalonia, eastern Aragón and parts of the Valencian Community.
  • They are usually made of stone and stand isolated or as part of a small complex.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Centre & South - White Towns
metas.note:
• Within the centre and south of Spain, towns made completely out of white painted houses are very common in Andalucía and Extremadura.
  • You can still see a fair amount of white painted houses in Castilla la Mancha but streets where every house is white will not be common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Galicia - Big Concrete Blocks
metas.note:
• Many houses in Galicia are built with big concrete blocks, sometimes textured to resemble natural stone.
  • Plain concrete blocks are also an extremely common material for walls and miscellaneous buildings like garages.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Galicia - Cabazos
metas.note:
• In Galicia, these unique granaries called “horreos gallegos”, or “cabazos”, are very common.
  • Note that they can be made from various materials, but the shape remains the same.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Northwest - Slate Roofs
metas.note:
• There is a large part of north-west Spain where you will find almost exclusively slate roofs (recognisable by their almost black colour).
  • This type of roofing can be seen sparingly all the way to the west coast of Galicia, but ends rather abruptly on the east.

--- NOTE:

  • Slate roofs can also be found in the Pyrenees near Andorra, and in the mountain ranges north east of Madrid.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Sri Lanka - Orange / Red Tiled Roofs
metas.note:
• Houses often have orange or red tiled roofs.
  • Due to wear and tear, these tiles often have an almost brown tint to them.

--- NOTE:

  • Similar roofs are also common in parts of Indonesia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sri-lanka.

metas.name: Sweden - Dalarna - Wooden Craftsmanship
metas.note:
• Central Dalarna has a strong tradition of wooden craftsmanship, and as a result much of the architecture has a unique, picturesque look to it.
  • Most commonly, you may find red timbered houses, portals made of logs, and so-called härbren which have a very distinct design.

--- NOTE:

  • Similar buildings can be found elsewhere in the country, but it is by far most common in central Dalarna.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Diamond Tiled Roofs
metas.note:
• Grey diamond-tiled roofs are mainly found in Skåne, Blekinge, Öland, and occasionally on Gotland.

--- NOTE:

  • Gotland and Öland are normally more easily recognised from landscape alone.
  • Houses in western and southern Skåne typically use a lot of stone and bricks, while houses in northeastern Skåne and Blekinge are mostly made of red painted wood.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - General Architecture
metas.note:
• Houses in the Swedish countryside are most commonly wooden and often painted with a distinct dark red paint, which is almost exclusively found in Sweden, Norway and Finland.
  • Urban architecture is usually modern and made of concrete and bricks, while suburban buildings are commonly freestanding single family houses built of either wood or brick.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Gotland - Limestone
metas.note:
• Houses on Gotland are commonly made of limestone and often have a dirty-looking white facade.
  • Churches on Gotland are very distinct looking, with either grey walls or white walls with grey corners, a large portal around the door and small windows typically divided in two by a pillar.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Grey Metal Roofs
metas.note:
• Grey metal roofs on residential buildings generally get more common the further north in the country you get.
  • Note that metal roofs on barns and sheds can be found significantly further south.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Hälsingland - Big Farmhouses
metas.note:
• Hälsingland has many big, mostly red, farmhouses.
  • They are characterised by many large windows, 2–3 floors, and the front facade being long and grand-looking.
  • Barns can also be seen having an unusual amount of windows in the region.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Northeast Coast - Octagonal Sheds
metas.note:
• Along the northern coast you will commonly encounter agricultural sheds which are either octagonal or rectangular, with the walls noticeably leaning outwards.
  • They will typically be made out of red-painted logs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Northwest Coast - Dense Shed Rows
metas.note: • Dense rows of very small red sheds are commonly found in coastal towns on the northern west coast.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Öland - Stone Bricks
metas.note: • This type of uneven stone brick is typically found in houses and rock walls on Öland, and less commonly in rock walls on Gotland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Skåne - Colored Triangle
metas.note:
• Houses in Skåne commonly have either a white stone, or a red brick wall with a coloured wooden triangle beneath the roof on the sides.
  • Similar houses with other materials (such as grey brick) for the walls can be found elsewhere in the southern half of the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Skåne - Red Bricks
metas.note:
• A lot of single family houses in Skåne are built out of red brick.
  • They typically look slightly older than red brick houses in other parts of the country.

--- NOTE:

  • Red brick architecture is also very common in Denmark.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - Skåne & Blekinge - Corrugated Moss Roofs
metas.note:
• Corrugated square metal roof panels with moss growing on them are typically found in southern Sweden, particularly in Skåne and Blekinge.
  • It is mainly found on large barns, and the roofs are often very steep.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - South Skåne - Half Timbered Houses
metas.note:
• Half-timbered houses can be found mainly in the southern half of Skåne, but also in the northern half and southern Halland.
  • It can also be found in Visby on rare occasions.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Sweden - West Coast - White Houses
metas.note:
• While houses in Sweden are mostly very colourful, on the west coast they are commonly much lighter.
  • There are an especially large number of white and light yellow houses along the coast between Gothenburg and the Norwegian border.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sweden.

metas.name: Switzerland - Alpine & Stone Buildings
metas.note:
• Swiss and Alpine architecture in general largely consists of stone buildings painted in light and warm colours, often combined with wooden parts and details.
  • Roofs are typically tiled and of a gable type.
  • It is extremely common for windows to have wooden shutters which open horizontally in two parts.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/switzerland.

metas.name: Switzerland - Appenzell - Barn Connections
metas.note:
• Around Appenzell, most houses will consist of a large living house connected to a long barn, such that the roof of the living house and the barn are at a 90° angle.
  • The front facade of the living house will often be divided into small squares, with each window being perfectly contained within a square.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/switzerland.

metas.name: Switzerland - Bern - Arch Shapes
metas.note: • Large houses with thick roofs, which are shaped like an arch underneath, are common around Bern.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/switzerland.

metas.name: Switzerland - Graubünden - Decorative Details
metas.note: • In the canton of Graubünden, you will often come across houses entirely made of stone, with, most commonly white, decorative painted details around windows and the edges of the house.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/switzerland.

metas.name: Switzerland - Northeast - Elaborate Timber Frames
metas.note:
• Elaborate timber frames, which are commonly painted red, are found in the northeast.

--- NOTE:

  • Simpler timber frames in other colours can be found in other parts of the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/switzerland.

metas.name: Switzerland - Ticino - Italian Architecture
metas.note:
• Not unexpectedly, seeing typical Italian architecture in Switzerland should imply that you are in the Italian-speaking areas in the south, principally the canton of Ticino.
  • The architectural style is characterized by, typically very smooth, orange-yellow stone walls with multiple floors and orange or brownish tiled roofs.
  • Green and brown Italian-style window shutters are common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/switzerland.

metas.name: Taiwan - General Architecture
metas.note:
• Architecture in Taiwan varies in designs, ranging from cramped, multiple-story housing to flat, single-story houses with backyards.
  • Many residential buildings have a very boxy look.
  • A lot of walls are covered in tiles, usually white.
  • Sheds made out of tin are also featured, commonly painted in a light green colour.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/taiwan.

metas.name: Taiwan - Kinmen - Traditional Architecture
metas.note: • You can find these small, traditional-looking houses in Kinmen.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/taiwan.

metas.name: Taiwan - North - Old & Disorganized Buildings
metas.note: • Old and disorganised housing units as well as tall dingy-looking apartment blocks are frequently seen in the urban areas of northern Taiwan.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/taiwan.

metas.name: Taiwan - Penghu - Cream Houses
metas.note: • White-tinged cream coloured houses are frequently seen in Penghu.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/taiwan.

metas.name: Taiwan - Taoyuan - Red Bricks
metas.note:
• Taoyuan features these red brick and sometimes red tile apartment buildings.

--- NOTE:

  • They can also be commonly spotted in the greater Taipei area and rarely in other urban areas but are most common in Taoyuan.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/taiwan.

metas.name: Taiwan - Yilan - Multiple-Story Villas
metas.note:
• In Yilan, you can find these rich multiple-story villas.
  • They come in all types of designs and are often gated.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/taiwan.

metas.name: Thailand - Corrugated Metal Roofs
metas.note: • Gray corrugated metal roofs are most commonly found in the north and south of the country, but can occasionally be found throughout the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/thailand.

metas.name: Tunisia - Traditional Blue Paint
metas.note:
• Doors, windows, gates and other architectural elements are sometimes painted with this specific traditional shade of blue.

--- NOTE:

  • This shade of blue can be found all over the country, but is especially common on the island of Djerba, where buildings tend to be older and more traditional.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/tunisia.

metas.name: Turkey - Apartment Blocks
metas.note: • Tall and somewhat square apartment blocks are very common in Turkey.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/turkey.

metas.name: Turkey - Batman - Spherical Water Tanks
metas.note: • White spherical water tanks can be found in the southeast, mainly south of Batman.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/turkey.

metas.name: Turkey - Central - Vertical Water Tanks
metas.note: • Vertical water tanks can be found in most of Turkey, but are notably uncommon along the south and west coast.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/turkey.

metas.name: Turkey - East - Metal Roofs
metas.note: • Metal roofs are most common in the east.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/turkey.

metas.name: Turkey - Lake Van - Pyramid Shapes
metas.note: • Sheet metal roofs shaped like low pyramids are mainly found far east, particularly in the general area surrounding Lake Van.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/turkey.

metas.name: Turkey - Nevşehir - Sandstone Bricks
metas.note: • Many buildings in the Nevşehir Province are built by large, light and unevenly coloured, sandstone bricks.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/turkey.

metas.name: Turkey - South - Square Water Tanks
metas.note: • Square water tanks with angled corners are found in the south, approximately from İskenderun to Sanliurfa.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/turkey.

metas.name: Turkey - South Coast - Flat Roofs
metas.note: • Flat roofs are mostly found in the southeast and to a lesser extent along the south coast.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/turkey.

metas.name: Turkey - South Coast - Horizontal Water Tanks
metas.note: • Horizontal water tanks placed on top of vertical water tanks are primarily found in a line following the south coast and going up to Elâzığ.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/turkey.

metas.name: Turkey - West - Tiled Roofs
metas.note:
• Tiled roofs are mostly found in the western two thirds of the country.
  • Note that for this and the following roof-related tips to be reliable, the majority of all visible roofs should preferably be of that type.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/turkey.

metas.name: Ukraine - Single Family Homes
metas.note:
• Single-family homes are very common in suburbs and small towns.
  • These neighbourhoods are often heavily vegetated and tend to look rundown.
  • Most roads are unpaved.
  • Buildings are usually made of bricks, often have corrugated roofs, and are invariably surrounded by fences.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ukraine.

metas.name: United Arab Emirates - Light-Colored Stone
metas.note:
• Houses in residential areas are typically made of light-coloured stone.
  • Reddish stones are often used for sidewalks.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-arab-emirates.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Chimney Pots
metas.note:
• Many British buildings have distinct-looking chimneys with multiple so-called chimney pots.
  • These pots are usually round and brick-coloured.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Identical Look
metas.note:
• Suburbs in UK towns tend to have a recognizable look.
  • They typically feature near-identical houses, often semi-detached, usually with well-manicured lawns.
  • The road layout can be maze-like, with lots of cul-de-sacs and curvy roads.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Red Bricks
metas.note:
• Red brick buildings are common in many parts of the UK.

--- NOTE:

  • Red brick architecture is also common in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Denmark, as well as parts of northern France.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Scotland - Sandstone & Granite
metas.note:
• It is common to see houses made of large blocks of sandstone or granite in Scotland.
  • Granite buildings are common in Aberdeen, red sandstone is common in Glasgow and Dumfries, and yellow sandstone is common in Edinburgh.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Terraced Houses
metas.note:
• Terraced houses (row houses) are very common in the UK.
  • This housing type shares walls on both sides with neighbouring homes.
  • You will also see a lot of semi-detached houses, which share just one side wall with another house.

--- NOTE:

  • 61% of the population lives in terraced or semi-detached houses, significantly more than most other European countries
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Timber Framing
metas.note:
• Some buildings, both old and new, feature black-and-white timber framing.

--- NOTE:

  • This is less common in Ireland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: Uruguay - Cube Shaped Houses
metas.note:
• Many Uruguayan houses are made out of concrete, and are somewhat cube-shaped.
  • Walls often have drab colours and tend to look weathered.
  • Flat roofs are relatively common.

--- NOTE:

  • Architecture in Argentina often looks similar.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/uruguay.

metas.name: US Virgin Islands - Unique Architecture
metas.note:
• A unique blend of architecture is found on the United States Virgin Islands.
  • The primary influences are European Renaissance, Spanish Baroque, Rococo and Victorian styles.
  • Facades with large arches are common, as well as central plazas and courtyards.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.
